title: EXTRA! EXTRA! The Newsboy Strike Episode!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover the New York newsboy strike of 1899, a roughly two-week walkout by New York City newsies (paper delivery boys) against the New York World and New York Journal, owned by Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst, over a bundle price increase imposed during the Spanish-American War. The episode covers the working conditions and economics of newsboys, the July 18 wagon tipping incident, the leaders (Dave Simons, Kid Blink, Racetrack Higgins), alleged payoffs to leaders, the New Irving Hall meeting, flyers and public support, the adult leadership of James Neil, the strike's end on August 1 with a return-unsold-copies deal at sixty cents per bundle, and the 1992 Disney musical Newsies. The episode ends with a listener mail complaint.
topics: Stuff You Missed in History Class

entities.name: Stuff You Missed in History Class

segments.title: Opening banter and Stuff You Missed in History Class
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the 1899 newsboy strike and note that a Stuff You Missed in History Class episode covered it in 2009.
topics: Stuff You Missed in History Class

segments.title: Who the newsboys were and their working lives
segments.summary: Newsboys were mostly working-class boys, some very young, who bought bundles of papers and resold them on their own. They paid fifty cents per bundle of one hundred, sold for a penny or more, and earned about thirty cents a day, roughly eleven dollars in today's money. Historical prices for everyday goods are compared.

segments.title: Street life and other cities' rules
segments.summary: Newsboys worked from sunup to sundown shouting headlines. New York had no rules unlike some other cities. The hosts describe the hardscrabble life of the boys and the background of the newspaper rivalry.

segments.title: Hearst, Pulitzer and the Spanish-American War price hike
segments.summary: During the Spanish-American War, the World and the Journal raised the bundle price from fifty to sixty cents. Other papers returned to prewar prices after circulation dropped, but the World and Journal did not. Context includes the Brooklyn and Manhattan trolley strike and earlier newsboy strikes in Boston, Dallas and Detroit.

segments.title: July 18 wagon tipping and the strike leaders
segments.summary: On July 18, 1899, newsboys in Queens and Long Island City tipped over a Journal delivery wagon after finding a driver stealing papers from their bundles. About three hundred boys rallied at City Hall Park. Leaders included Dave Simons, Lewis Biletti (Kid Blink) and Racetrack Higgins; other nicknames are mentioned.

segments.title: Strike begins and violence against scabs
segments.summary: On July 20 the newsboys were told to stop selling the World and Journal, with threats. Boys carried clubs and beat sellers of those papers. Police made a few arrests while busy with the trolley strike. On July 24 a fourteen-year-old led a marching crowd chanting against the papers.

segments.title: Ticker tape parade, fire hydrant and spread of the strike
segments.summary: Strikers marched down Wall Street where brokerage workers threw ticker tape. A street cleaner turned on a fire hydrant. The strike spread to New Jersey, Connecticut and Rhode Island, and women newspaper sellers joined.
topics: New Jersey Connecticut Rhode Island strikes

segments.title: Newspapers' response and use of adult scabs
segments.summary: Advertisers worried about lost readership and the World's managing editor Don Sites said the public was against the paper. The papers tried to hire homeless adults as scabs, about one hundred signed up but did not show up the next morning.

segments.title: July 24 meeting at New Irving Hall
segments.summary: Hearst refused to meet the arbitration committee. About two thousand (reports range up to eight thousand) attended the meeting at New Irving Hall, chaired by Nick Myers with muscle including Joe Bernstein and William Reese. Racetrack Higgins gave a speech; he said the Journal had offered two dollars a day.

segments.title: Flyers and changing tactics
segments.summary: Strikers decided to stop beating scabs and instead distributed flyers appealing to New Yorkers' sense of justice, which helped turn public opinion.

segments.title: Spread to other cities and the papers' silence
segments.summary: Sympathetic strikes arose in Nashville, Lexington and Cincinnati, spread largely by word of mouth and by other newspapers covering the strike. The World and Journal did not publish about the strike.

segments.title: Alleged payoffs to Kid Blink and Dave Simons
segments.summary: Kid Blink and Dave Simons were allegedly paid about four hundred dollars by the two papers to end the strike; both denied it. Simons resigned as president, and leadership became unclear as papers named different leaders. On July 27 Kid Blink appeared in a new suit flashing money, and was arrested, possibly for his protection. Racetrack Higgins is noted as not bought off.

segments.title: Adult leadership, decline, and end of the strike
segments.summary: Newsstand owner Abraham Lippmann helped elect James Neil, fifty, as president, with Racetrack Higgins as vice president. Organization was too late as the boys ran out of money. Newsstand groups dropped support on July 31 and the strike officially ended August 1.

segments.title: Settlement terms and the newsboy union legacy
segments.summary: The papers accepted a deal of sixty cents per bundle with the right to return unsold copies for a full refund. The union continued, grew and supported later strikes.

segments.title: Newsies the 1992 Disney musical
segments.summary: Disney released the 1992 musical Newsies, with Christian Bale playing fictional character Jack Kelly, with characters Blink and Race based on real strikers. The film was a commercial flop but a cult hit and later became a Broadway show with two Tonys.

segments.title: Listener mail on tone and bias
segments.summary: An anonymous listener criticized the hosts for laughing too much and for supporting the Black Panther Party. The hosts said they would not change the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and listener mail address.
